source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris
framing: Gap framing: every figure is what is NOT covered, NOT satisfied or unmet. Gap figures are 100 minus the published figure.
rule: HAL may phrase these facts freely but must not state any figure, ranking or claim that is not in this list. Verbatim report sentences may name other countries; only what they say about this country may be used.

facts.text: 29% of people in Slovenia were NOT satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 36%; satisfaction has deteriorated over the past decade.
26.4% of health spending in Slovenia was NOT covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 24.9%.
3.4% of people in Slovenia reported unmet medical care needs due to cost, distance or waiting times in 2024 (average of 28 OECD countries: 3.4%).
13% of hospital care costs in Slovenia were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 11% on average in the OECD.
22% of outpatient medical care costs in Slovenia were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 22% on average in the OECD.
53% of dental care costs in Slovenia were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 68% on average in the OECD.
49% of pharmaceutical costs in Slovenia were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 42% on average in the OECD.
In Slovenia, a major policy reform in 2024 replaced its complementary insurance with a new compulsory healthcare contribution as part of its social health insurance system.

This varies considerably across OECD countries, from fewer than 2% of households experiencing catastrophic health spending in Sweden, Slovenia, the United Kingdom, Ireland and the Netherlands, to over 10% of households in Lithuania, Latvia and Hungary (Figure 5.10).
In terms of median number of days (Figure 5.11, right panel), this ranged from around 50 days or less in Spain, Poland, Hungary and Sweden, to 280 days in Slovenia.
However, in New Zealand and Slovenia, waiting times have continued to increase on both metrics since the pandemic.
In 2024, median waiting times ranged from 67 days in Sweden and Spain, to over half a year in Hungary (209 days), Chile (313 days), Poland (343 days), and almost two years in Slovenia (667 days).
Furthermore, waiting times have remained above pre-pandemic levels in more countries, with large increases observed in Slovenia.
Iceland, Portugal, Italy, Korea and Sweden reported rates lower than 12 per 100 000 population, while Chile, Czechia, Slovenia and Germany reported rates higher than 40 per 100 000.
By contrast, countries including France, Slovenia and Spain have lower price levels, with the same healthcare basket costing roughly two-thirds of the OECD average.

Meanwhile, in Slovenia, Poland and Costa Rica, the role of government transfers in funding compulsory insurance schemes is marginal, with social insurance contributions representing at least 90% of all revenues of these schemes.
